 India Prohibits Battery Black Mass Exports
 Star marking (1-5) indicates the importance of topic for CSE -->
 20 Nov 2026 
 8 min read
 Tags: Quick Facts For Prelims 
 GS Paper - 3 
 Mobilization of Resources 
 Source: IE   
 Why in News? 
 The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has amended India’s export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ with immediate effect to retain mineral-rich battery waste domestically and strengthen India’s critical mineral recycling and refining ecosystem .    
 What is Black Mass?   
 Black Mass: It is a powder-like residue left after shredding and breaking down waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics.    
 It acts as a vital secondary source of critical minerals , containing lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite, silicon, tin, and rhenium .   
 Chemistry-Dependent Value: Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) batteries yield high-value nickel and cobalt, whereas Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries, increasingly used in Electric Vehicles (EVs) and energy storage, contain iron and phosphate, making them less lucrative for recyclers.    
 Regulatory Framework: The Technical Review Committee (TRC) of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) classifies black mass as hazardous waste (unless processed on-site).    
 The Basel Convention (1989) regulates the transboundary movement of hazardous waste, including lithium-ion battery black mass, ensuring environmentally sound management and controlled cross-border trade.    
 India implements its obligations through the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016.   
 Urban Mining & Recovery Methods of Black Mass: Recovering minerals from discarded products already in circulation is known as Urban Mining.   
 Pyrometallurgy: Uses high-temperature smelting to extract nickel, cobalt, and copper; it is energy-intensive and often loses valuable minerals like lithium in the slag.   
 Hydrometallurgy: Uses chemical solutions (leaching, solvent extraction, crystallisation) to recover battery-grade compounds ( lithium hydroxide, nickel sulphate, cobalt sulphate ). It is favoured by NITI Aayog for higher recovery rates and lower energy consumption.   
 Objective of the Export Ban: The move ensures feedstock availability for domestic recycling and refining units, improves capacity utilisation, promotes domestic value addition , and generates investment and employment in India’s circular economy.   
 India’s decision aligns with a broader global push for resource security , following a year-long export ban on black mass by the United States and upcoming restrictions by the European Union .   
 High Import Dependence: India has limited domestic reserves and processing capacity, making it nearly 100% import-dependent for key minerals like lithium, cobalt, nickel, silicon, and Rare Earth Elements (REEs) .   
 China controls 90% of global critical mineral processing and frequently uses export restrictions as geopolitical leverage during trade tensions with the US and Europe.   
 Domestic Potential: India generates ~ 50,000 tonnes of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries annually (~ 25,000 tonnes of black mass), most of which was previously exported to China and South Korea for refining.   
 As of November 2026, India had 57 CPCB -registered lithium-ion battery recyclers , with an annual processing capacity of 5.17 lakh metric tonnes (MT) and black mass input capacity of 75,500 MT .    
 A January 2026 NITI Aayog–TERI report notes that India’s battery demand will jump from 16 gigawatt-hours (GWh) (2023) to 248 GWh (2035) , while recyclable batteries will surge from 19,000 to 233,000 tonnes , creating a vast domestic resource pool for critical mineral processing.   
 Policy Ecosystem: Complementing the ban, in November 2026, the Centre approved a Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing to build a self-reliant critical mineral ecosystem.   
 Policy Challenge: The export ban can improve domestic feedstock availability but must be complemented by advanced refining infrastructure, commercially viable mineral recovery, stronger EPR incentives and environmental safeguards to develop a sustainable circular economy.   
 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)   
 1. What is black mass, and why is it important for critical mineral security?
 Black mass is the powder-like residue obtained from shredding waste lithium-ion batteries. It contains valuable secondary minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, making it an important resource for domestic mineral recovery.   
 2. Why has India prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass?
 The DGFT changed its export policy from 'Free' to 'Prohibited' to retain domestic feedstock, improve recycling capacity utilisation, promote indigenous refining and reduce import dependence on critical minerals.   
 3. What is the difference between pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy?
 Pyrometallurgy: Uses high-temperature smelting to recover metals but is energy-intensive and may lose lithium in slag.   
 Hydrometallurgy: Uses chemical leaching and extraction processes to recover battery-grade compounds with higher recovery rates and lower energy consumption.   
 4. What are the key provisions of the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022?
 The Rules mandate Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), prohibit landfill disposal of batteries and establish minimum recycled-content targets to promote environmentally sound battery recycling.   
 UPSC Civil Services Examination Previous Year Question (PYQ) 
 Prelims :     
 Q1. Consider the following minerals: (2020)      
 Bentonite     
 Chromite     
 Kyanite     
 Sillimanite     
 In India, which of the above is/are officially designated as major minerals?   
 (A) 1 and 2 only     
 (B) 4 only     
 (C) 1 and 3 only     
 (D) 2, 3 and 4 only     
 Ans: D      
 Q2.Recently, there has been a concern over the short supply of a group of elements called ‘rare earth metals’. Why? (2012)      
 China, which is the largest producer of these elements, has imposed some restrictions on their export.     
 Other than China, Australia, Canada and Chile, these elements are not found in any country.     
 Rare earth metals are essential for the manufacture of various kinds of electronic items and there is a growing demand for these elements.     
 Which of the statements given above is/are correct?      
 (A) 1 only     
 (B) 2 and 3 only     
 (C) 1 and 3 only     
 (D) 1, 2 and 3     
 Ans: C
